topic: A list of research and dissertation topics: the discriminant and invariants of the quartic, Poincaré cycles of differential equations, rotation of a body filled with fluid, three number-theoretic doctoral topics (class fields, Fermat's theorem, Weber's theorem), and independence of the laws 1-17 for complex number systems.

triage.modern_statement: This is most likely the question of how many limit cycles ('Cykel' in Poincaré's sense, i.e. closed trajectories) a planar polynomial ODE x' = P(x,y), y' = Q(x,y) of degree n can have. Put another way: find the maximum number H(n) of limit cycles, and their relative positions, for planar polynomial vector fields of degree n. The note is only three words, so this reading rests on where it sits: under the page's item on 'Poincaré cycles of differential equations'.
triage.answered_by: Not answered in general. Hilbert included it as the second part of his 16th problem (Paris ICM, 1900). Ilyashenko and Écalle, working independently in the early 1990s, proved that every single planar polynomial vector field has only finitely many limit cycles. No uniform upper bound H(n) is known for any n > 1. Even whether H(2) = 4 is still open; the only value known is the trivial H(1) = 0.

evidence.claim: The second part of Hilbert's 16th problem asks for an upper bound on the number of limit cycles of degree-n planar polynomial vector fields and their relative positions. No upper bound is known for any n > 1.

Ilyashenko and Écalle independently proved, in the early 1990s, that any given planar polynomial vector field has finitely many limit cycles. Whether H(2) = 4 is still open, and research on the problem is still very active.
A 2007 BIRS workshop report describes the second part of Hilbert's 16th problem as completely open. It notes that per-field finiteness gives no uniform estimate.
The only known Hilbert number is H(1) = 0.
A 2024 paper proves that H(n) is a strictly increasing function whenever it is finite, which shows work on the problem continues.

triage.why: On a page that lists 'Poincaré cycles of differential equations', the question 'how many cycles' best fits the problem of counting limit cycles. Hilbert made this the second half of his 16th problem in 1900. The sources say it is unsolved even for quadratic systems and still actively studied. Confidence is medium, not high, because the note is so short: it could also be a narrower question about one specific equation from Poincaré's work, and the sources cannot rule that out.
